author: Claude (English teacher role)
basis: Original A2 kept, except the four slides whose vocabulary pushed the mission above the A2 band (FK 7.8). Only those lines are simplified; facts unchanged.

slides.1: Good morning. Before we talk about poverty far away, look around us. Poverty can hide in a classmate who skips lunch, or a student with no quiet place to study.
slides.2: SDG 1 means ending poverty in all its forms. It is not only about income. It is also about safety, health care, education, housing, and the chance to recover when life becomes difficult.
slides.3: In Taiwan, many students have good schools and technology. But not every family has the same support. Some families struggle with rent, medical costs, or unstable jobs.
slides.4: The first challenge is working poverty. Some people work hard but still cannot feel secure. Temporary jobs, low wages, and long hours make planning difficult. If parents are stressed, children's learning can also be affected.
slides.5: Housing is another pressure. When rent is high, families may spend less on food, books, tutoring, or transportation. Students might move often or live in crowded rooms. A stable home is part of learning.
slides.6: Poverty also appears online. Some students have fast internet, laptops, and parents who can help. Others share one phone or cannot join online learning easily. Digital gaps become learning gaps.
slides.7: Taiwan has safety nets. We have social help, health insurance, and local services. These protect basic needs. But does help arrive before a small problem becomes a crisis?
slides.8: Schools can reduce poverty's effect on children. Meal programs, scholarships, counseling, after-school support, and teachers who notice students early are all important. School is not only a classroom. It can be a support system.
slides.9: Community groups also help. Food banks, social workers, religious groups, NGOs, and volunteer teams can find needs that official systems miss. But charity alone is not enough. Long-term support must build skills and dignity.
slides.10: One solution is financial literacy. Students can learn budgeting, saving, responsible borrowing, and how to avoid scams. These skills do not solve poverty alone, but they help young people make safer choices in the future.
slides.11: Technology can also help. Students can use simple data maps to understand where help is needed: food access, public transportation, elderly care, or after-school programs. Data should guide kindness, not replace it.
slides.12: Service learning connects English, SDGs, and action. Students can interview local groups, write bilingual posters, design donation guides, or teach younger students. The best learning is not only speaking about problems, but working with people.
slides.13: Poverty may grow as Taiwan gets older. Old people who live alone need care, money, and transport. Poverty is linked to health, family, and public services.
slides.14: Migrant workers and new immigrant families also need fair access. Language and paperwork make services hard to use. Good support helps their children and adults join society.
slides.15: Climate disasters can make poverty worse. Floods and extreme heat hurt low-income families first, because they have less money to fall back on. SDG 1 and climate action are linked.
slides.16: Finally, we must talk about dignity. Helping people should not make them feel ashamed. If we only see poor people as weak, we miss their strengths. Real support listens, respects, and works together.
slides.17: To sum up, SDG 1 is about shared security. Poverty affects education, health, housing, and dreams. Taiwan has support systems, but we still need earlier help, better access, and stronger community action.
slides.18: We also need to challenge stereotypes. It is easy to blame poor people, but poverty is often caused by low wages, high costs, illness, care duties, or disasters. Understanding the system helps us respond wisely.
slides.19: Young people can help by building skills, networks, and voice. We can learn English to share SDG ideas, use data to explain problems, and join local projects. Small actions become powerful when they are organized.
slides.20: Thank you for listening. SDG 1 asks us to see poverty clearly and to act with respect. Let us start from our own school and our own words.
